questions.definition: A step-by-step method for solving a problem or completing a task.
questions.clue: Often written before coding begins.
questions.explanation: An algorithm describes the logical steps needed to solve a problem. It can be shown using pseudocode, flowcharts, or structured English before it is turned into program code.

questions.definition: A number system that uses only 0 and 1.
questions.clue: Computers store data using this system.
questions.explanation: Binary is base 2. Computers use binary because digital circuits can reliably represent two states, such as on and off.

questions.definition: The smallest unit of data in a computer.
questions.clue: It stores one binary digit.
questions.explanation: A bit can hold either 0 or 1. Larger units such as bytes are made from groups of bits.

questions.definition: A unit of data usually made up of 8 bits.
questions.clue: Often used to store one character.
questions.explanation: A byte contains 8 bits. File sizes and memory capacity are often measured in bytes, kilobytes, megabytes, and gigabytes.

questions.definition: A named storage location whose value can change while a program runs.
questions.clue: Used to hold data in a program.
questions.explanation: A variable stores a value that a program can read or update. For example, a score variable may increase during a game.

questions.definition: A named value that should not change while a program runs.
questions.clue: The opposite of a variable.
questions.explanation: A constant is useful for values that stay the same, such as VAT rate or maximum score. Naming constants makes code easier to read and maintain.

questions.definition: Repeating a set of instructions in a program.
questions.clue: Loops are used for this.
questions.explanation: Iteration means repetition. A program may use a for loop, while loop, or repeat loop to run instructions more than once.

questions.definition: Choosing which instructions to run based on a condition.
questions.clue: Uses IF, THEN, ELSE logic.
questions.explanation: Selection lets a program make decisions. For example, an if statement can check whether a password is correct before allowing access.

questions.definition: Instructions carried out one after another in order.
questions.clue: The simplest programming structure.
questions.explanation: Sequence means the order of steps matters. Programs normally execute instructions from top to bottom unless selection or iteration changes the flow.

questions.definition: A way of planning an algorithm using code-like language that is not tied to one programming language.
questions.clue: Readable by humans, not normally run by a computer.
questions.explanation: Pseudocode helps programmers focus on logic before syntax. It is commonly used in exams to describe algorithms clearly.

questions.definition: A diagram that shows the steps and decisions in an algorithm.
questions.clue: Uses symbols such as process boxes and decision diamonds.
questions.explanation: A flowchart is a visual way to represent an algorithm. It shows the order of steps and where decisions or loops occur.

questions.definition: Data entered into a computer system.
questions.clue: A keyboard and mouse can provide this.
questions.explanation: Input is data provided to a system for processing. Examples include typed text, sensor readings, and button presses.

questions.definition: Information produced by a computer system after processing.
questions.clue: A monitor or printer can display this.
questions.explanation: Output is the result produced by a computer. It might be shown on screen, printed, stored, or sent to another device.

questions.definition: The component that executes instructions and processes data.
questions.clue: Also called the CPU.
questions.explanation: The processor, or CPU, fetches, decodes, and executes instructions. It is a central part of a computer system.

questions.definition: Temporary memory used to store programs and data currently in use.
questions.clue: Its contents are lost when power is turned off.
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile memory. It allows quick access to data and instructions while a computer is running.

questions.definition: Non-volatile memory that stores instructions needed to start a computer.
questions.clue: Its contents remain when power is turned off.
questions.explanation: ROM keeps its data without power. It often stores firmware or boot instructions used when a device starts.

questions.definition: A translator that converts a whole program into machine code before it is run.
questions.clue: Produces executable code.
questions.explanation: A compiler translates source code into machine code. Errors are usually reported after compilation, before the program runs.

questions.definition: A translator that runs a program one instruction at a time.
questions.clue: Often used while testing code.
questions.explanation: An interpreter translates and executes code line by line. This can make testing easier, but execution may be slower than compiled code.

questions.definition: Checking that data is reasonable and follows expected rules.
questions.clue: For example, checking a date is in the correct range.
questions.explanation: Validation checks whether input is acceptable, such as ensuring a number is within a range. It does not prove the data is true.

questions.definition: Checking that data has been copied or entered accurately.
questions.clue: Double entry is one method.
questions.explanation: Verification checks that data matches the original source. For example, entering an email address twice can help detect typing errors.
